title: JPMorgan Sees CBRT Room to Start Cutting in September as Ankara Finalizes Medium-Term Program
subhead: Wall Street now expects Turkey's central bank to begin easing next month, with JPMorgan forecasting a year-end policy rate of 35 percent, while Ankara finalizes its medium-term economic program ahead of the 2027 budget.

sections.heading: Rate Cut Bets Firm as JPMorgan Sees Disinflation Space
sections.body:
JPMorgan says Türkiye's inflation outlook now gives the Central Bank of the Republic of Türkiye (CBRT) room to begin cutting interest rates in September, according to a daily investor note covered by Türkiye Today citing Matriks Haber. The bank argues that July inflation coming in below expectations, weakening inflation momentum and an improvement in the current account balance created space to ease without a fundamental change to exchange rate policy.

JPMorgan economist Fatih Akcelik expects the CBRT to resume one-week repo auctions next month and then cut the policy rate by 100 basis points each in October and December, bringing it to 35 percent by year-end, per BloombergHT. In its Aug. 21 note, JPMorgan forecast monthly inflation of 1.9 percent in August, led by fuel prices, with annual headline inflation at 31.6 percent. Akcelik said tight financial conditions were expected to keep weighing on household consumption.
sections.whyItMatters: A September easing would mark the first rate cut in a coordinated disinflation program, signaling that officials and investors believe the inflation fight has reached a durable turning point — a bet that hinges on oil prices, lira stability and the incoming US financial measures on Iran.

sections.heading: Hot Money and the Carry-Trade Risk
sections.body:
JPMorgan identified market positioning as the main risk to the easing path, estimating foreign-sourced carry trade positions at about $47 billion — above pre-Iran-conflict levels — and warning that this reduces markets' capacity to absorb negative surprises from domestic politics, inflation or energy prices. The bank noted that financial measures US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent is expected to announce against Iran on Monday are being closely watched and have already contributed to recent outflows from the lira.

Separately, Türkiye's Treasury and Finance Ministry is exploring tax options to steer short-term flows out of money market funds, which have drawn foreign investors seeking carry returns, Bloomberg HT reported. Money market fund capitalization has ballooned from ₺77.5 billion in May 2023 to ₺1.8 trillion in July 2026, roughly a 2,269 percent increase, as high domestic rates made short-term instruments attractive. The ministry is weighing whether to extend withholding treatment beyond the current 17.5 percent rate on individual money-market fund income, which does not apply to institutional investors.
sections.whyItMatters: Ankara is trying to turn short-term, hot-money inflows into longer-term investment at the very moment the carry trade has surged past pre-crisis levels — a balancing act that could go wrong if rate cuts trigger a reversal of those flows.

sections.heading: Medium-Term Program Finalized Ahead of 2027 Budget
sections.body:
Officials are finalizing Turkey's Medium-Term Program (MTP) ahead of the 2027 budget rollout, with Hürriyet Daily News and Azerbaijani state media reporting that the economic roadmap is being put into its final form. The program is expected to set the fiscal and monetary framework for the coming years, formalizing targets that underpin the recent disinflation and carry-trade strategy.

The timing is notable: the roadmap is being locked down just as investors begin pricing rate cuts and as the central bank's reserve and carry-trade dynamics are under renewed scrutiny.
sections.whyItMatters: The MTP will translate the central bank's monetary tightening into a multi-year fiscal and inflation framework, effectively committing the next phase of economic policy — and the market's view of it — to paper.

sections.heading: US Envoy Publicly Undercuts Israel's Syria Strike Justification
sections.body:
The top US envoy for the region has publicly contradicted Israel's rationale for its recent strike on a Syrian airbase, telling Israeli media the strike was 'election-related' and intended to 'bait' Ankara into confrontation, according to Haaretz and The Jerusalem Post. The envoy's comments align with the broader US push for a deconfliction mechanism among Turkey, Israel and Syria, which Reuters reported Washington is working on — a mechanism that Israel has so far resisted, per i24NEWS.

Former Israeli officials have also warned the strike risked a military confrontation with Turkey, with The Jerusalem Post noting the incident has sharply raised the stakes in the Israel-Turkey standoff over Syria.
sections.whyItMatters: Washington's public airing of a rift with Israel over the strike, combined with the deconfliction push, signals the US is trying to control a Turkey-Israel escalation it views as dangerously risky — even as Israel resists constraints.

sections.heading: PKK Peace Process: Criticism Over Law's Limited Scope
sections.body:
Days after President Erdogan signed the conditional pardon law for PKK militants (reported by The Washington Post on Aug. 18), a senior PKK figure has criticized the law's limited scope, Turkish Minute reports. The legislation, part of the dissolution process that began when the PKK announced its dissolution in May 2025 and members started destroying weapons in northern Iraq two months later, does not specify the fate of imprisoned PKK founder Abdullah Öcalan.

Vice President Cevdet Yılmaz said before the law's passage that Öcalan's case fell outside the legislation's scope, while leaving open the possibility he could continue contributing to the peace process. Separately, senior PKK commanders have reiterated that Öcalan's freedom is key to lasting peace, per Rudaw.
sections.whyItMatters: The gap between the pardon law's mechanics and Kurdish demands over Öcalan's status remains the central unresolved fault line in a peace process that has moved from armed conflict to legal and political bargaining.

sections.heading: Armenia Looks Toward Energy Links With Turkey and Azerbaijan
sections.body:
In a region of Ankara's periphery, Armenian authorities are looking into establishing energy links with Turkey and Azerbaijan, the Armenian news agency Arka.am reported. The development follows Turkey's broader push into regional energy integration, including the 'four seas' energy vision Ankara and Damascus announced in the strategic council with Syria earlier in the week.

The Armenian interest, while at an early stage, touches the same web of post-Caucasus normalization and energy connectivity politics that Ankara has been advancing across the Caucasus and Central Asia.
sections.whyItMatters: Any concrete Armenia-Turkey-Azerbaijan energy tie would mark a meaningful step in Caucasus normalization, giving Ankara another lever in its campaign to position itself as a regional energy hub while reducing its reliance on volatile external transit routes.

bottomLine: The dominant story of the past week — Turkey's confrontation with Israel over Syria — has not materially changed, so the day's real news is economic. JPMorgan now expects the CBRT to start cutting rates in September and to reach 35 percent by year-end, betting that disinflation is durable enough to ease without breaking the lira's real-appreciation strategy. That bet sits against a backdrop of record carry trade, a Treasury exploring new taxes on hot money, and the finalization of the Medium-Term Program ahead of the 2027 budget. Meanwhile Washington's public rebuke of Israel's Syria strike and the push for a three-way deconfliction mechanism, along with quiet movement on the PKK peace law and Armenian energy overtures, round out a day where policy planning — not headlines — defined Turkey's position.
sources: Türkiye Today, Bloomberg HT, JPMorgan (via Türkiye Today), Hürriyet Daily News, Azərtac, AzerNews, Reuters, Haaretz, The Jerusalem Post, i24NEWS, The Washington Post, Turkish Minute, Rudaw, Arka.am
